results.name: Tacos al Pastor
results.locality: Mexico City (originated in CDMX, La Condesa area)
results.short_description: Marinated pork cooked on a vertical spit (*trompo*), shaved to order and served with pineapple, onion, and cilantro on double-stacked corn tortillas. Evolved from Lebanese/Syrian shawarma traditions brought to Mexico; the taco version was invented in CDMX circa 1966.
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★★★ — Undisputed signature dish of the city

results.name: Tacos de Suadero
results.short_description: Slow-cooked beef brisket (*suadero*), rendered until soft with slightly crispy edges, served in corn tortillas. Described as a CDMX specialty rarely found elsewhere in Mexico. Featured in Netflix's *Las Crónicas del Taco*.

results.name: Tacos de Canasta
results.locality: Mexico City (Centro Histórico, metro stations, markets)
results.short_description: "Basket tacos" — small, soft tacos steamed inside a cloth-lined basket, typically filled with beans, potato, chicharrón, or mole. Originated as practical food for workers and are sold from bicycles and carts throughout the city.

results.name: Pambazo
results.short_description: A bread roll dipped and fried in red guajillo chile sauce, filled with potatoes and chorizo, then topped with lettuce, cream, and cheese. A bold, spicy street-food staple of CDMX markets and fondas.
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★★ — Strongly associated with CDMX street stalls

results.name: Tlacoyo
results.locality: Mexico City and Valley of Mexico
results.short_description: Thick, oval-shaped corn masa patty (often blue corn) stuffed with beans, cheese, or fava beans, then toasted on a comal and topped with salsa, nopales, and cream. Pre-Hispanic origins tied to the Basin of Mexico.
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★★ — Ancient Valley of Mexico staple, ubiquitous at CDMX markets

results.name: Quesadilla (CDMX-style)
results.short_description: Pressed corn-masa turnover with a wide range of fillings — huitlacoche, flor de calabaza (squash blossom), chicharrón, or cheese. Famously, in CDMX a quesadilla does *not* necessarily contain cheese (a source of national debate).
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★★ — The "quesadilla sin queso" is a uniquely chilango phenomenon

results.name: Chilaquiles
results.short_description: Fried tortilla chips bathed in green or red salsa, topped with cream, cheese, onion, and often a fried egg or shredded chicken. A beloved CDMX morning staple served at fondas and market stalls across the city.

results.name: Esquites
results.short_description: Corn kernels cut from the cob and served warm in a cup with mayonnaise, lime, chili powder, and cotija cheese. While corn snacks exist nationwide, the cup-served esquites format is especially emblematic of CDMX street corners.
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★ — Widely associated with CDMX street culture

results.name: Torta (CDMX-style)
results.short_description: Hearty sandwich on a *telera* or *bolillo* roll, stuffed with fillings like milanesa, ham, or al pastor meat, plus avocado, beans, and jalapeños. While tortas exist across Mexico, the CDMX urban torta tradition — especially late-night torta stands — is a distinct local institution.
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★★ — Evolved into an iconic CDMX urban staple

results.name: Tamales (CDMX morning tradition)
results.locality: Mexico City (metro stations, morning street vendors)
results.short_description: Steamed corn-dough parcels filled with mole, rajas, or sweet fillings, wrapped in corn husks. In CDMX they are uniquely served inside a bolillo roll as a *guajolota* (tamale torta) — a carb-on-carb combination that is distinctly chilango.
results.strength_of_local_association: ★★★★★ — The *guajolota* is exclusively a Mexico City creation
